domain.name: Data Scientist
domain.description: From statistics and programming to machine learning and production data science.

skills.name: Python for Data Science
skills.description: Use Python, pandas, and numpy for analysis, scripting, and modeling.

skills.name: Probability
skills.description: Random variables, distributions, conditional probability, and Bayes' theorem.

skills.name: Descriptive Statistics
skills.description: Summarize data with central tendency, dispersion, and distribution shape.

skills.name: Linear Algebra
skills.description: Vectors, matrices, matrix operations, and eigenvalues for ML.

skills.name: Data Wrangling
skills.description: Clean, reshape, join, and aggregate messy real-world data.

skills.name: Exploratory Data Analysis
skills.description: Investigate datasets to surface patterns, anomalies, and hypotheses.

skills.name: Data Visualization
skills.description: Communicate findings with clear, accurate, and honest charts.

skills.name: Inferential Statistics
skills.description: Draw conclusions about populations from samples.

skills.name: SQL for Analysis
skills.description: Query and transform data in relational databases for analysis.

skills.name: Regression Analysis
skills.description: Model continuous outcomes with linear and regularized regression.

skills.name: Classification
skills.description: Predict discrete outcomes with logistic regression, trees, and SVM.

skills.name: Feature Engineering
skills.description: Create, select, and transform features to boost model performance.

skills.name: Model Evaluation
skills.description: Assess models with cross-validation, appropriate metrics, and error analysis.

skills.name: Experimental Design
skills.description: Design controlled experiments with proper randomization and power.

skills.name: A/B Testing
skills.description: Run and analyze controlled experiments to make data-driven decisions.

skills.name: Clustering
skills.description: Group similar observations with K-means, DBSCAN, and hierarchical methods.

skills.name: Time Series Analysis
skills.description: Model trends, seasonality, and forecast future values.

skills.name: Causal Inference
skills.description: Estimate causal effects from observational data using DAGs and methods like IV, DiD.

skills.name: ML in Production
skills.description: Deploy, monitor, and maintain models in real-world systems.

skills.name: Data Science Communication
skills.description: Translate technical findings into business decisions stakeholders act on.

questions.prompt: Which pandas method reads a CSV file into a DataFrame?
questions.explanation: pd.read_csv() is the canonical loader for CSV files. Also pd.read_parquet, pd.read_json, etc.

questions.prompt: Which pandas method returns the number of rows in a DataFrame?
questions.explanation: df.shape returns (rows, cols), so df.shape[0] is the row count. len(df) also works.

questions.prompt: If events A and B are independent, then P(A ∩ B) equals:
questions.explanation: Independence means the joint probability factors into the product of marginals.

questions.prompt: Bayes' theorem states that P(A|B) equals:
questions.explanation: P(A|B) = P(B|A) · P(A) / P(B). It updates a prior belief given new evidence.

questions.prompt: Which measure is least sensitive to outliers?
questions.explanation: The median is the middle value, so extreme values barely shift it.

questions.prompt: Standard deviation is the square root of:
questions.explanation: Std dev = √variance, restoring the original units of the data.

questions.prompt: The dot product of two orthogonal vectors is:
questions.explanation: Orthogonal (perpendicular) vectors have a dot product of zero.

questions.prompt: An eigenvector of matrix A satisfies:

options.text: Av = λv for some scalar λ

questions.explanation: The matrix only scales eigenvectors; the scale factor is the eigenvalue.

questions.prompt: In pandas, which method merges two DataFrames on a common column?
questions.explanation: pd.merge() implements SQL-style joins (inner, left, right, outer) on shared keys.

questions.prompt: Which is the correct order of the split-apply-combine pattern in pandas?
questions.explanation: groupby splits rows by key, you aggregate (sum, mean, etc.), and pandas combines results.

questions.prompt: A histogram is best used to show:

options.text: Distribution of a single numeric variable

questions.explanation: Histograms bin a single numeric variable and reveal shape, skew, and modality.

questions.prompt: The Interquartile Range (IQR) is computed as:
questions.explanation: IQR = 75th percentile minus 25th percentile. Robust measure of spread.

questions.prompt: A correlation of −0.8 between two variables means:
questions.explanation: |r| near 1 means strong linear association; the negative sign means they move in opposite directions.

questions.prompt: Which chart best shows the relationship between two continuous variables?
questions.explanation: Scatter plots display paired continuous values, exposing correlation, clusters, and outliers.

questions.prompt: The Central Limit Theorem states that:

options.text: The sampling distribution of the mean approaches normality as sample size grows

questions.explanation: CLT justifies using normal-based inference on sample means even for skewed populations.

questions.prompt: A 95% confidence interval for a mean means:

options.text: 95% of the data lies in this interval
~95% of such intervals would contain the true mean over repeated experiments

questions.explanation: It describes long-run coverage of the interval-building procedure, not a probability for one specific interval.

questions.prompt: Which SQL clause filters rows after aggregation?
questions.explanation: WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters aggregated groups after GROUP BY.

questions.prompt: A LEFT JOIN between tables A and B returns:

options.text: All rows of A plus matching rows of B (nulls if no match)

questions.explanation: LEFT JOIN preserves every row of the left table; right-side columns are NULL where there's no match.

questions.prompt: In linear regression, R² measures:

options.text: Proportion of variance in the target explained by the model

questions.explanation: R² ranges from −∞ to 1; higher is better. R² = 1 means perfect fit.

questions.prompt: Multicollinearity in regression means:

options.text: Predictors are highly correlated with each other

questions.explanation: Correlated predictors make coefficient estimates unstable. VIF detects it; ridge regression or dropping features can fix it.

questions.prompt: Which metric is best for a heavily imbalanced binary classification task?
questions.explanation: Accuracy is misleading when one class dominates. AUC-ROC and PR-AUC measure ranking quality independent of threshold.

questions.prompt: In logistic regression, the sigmoid function:
questions.explanation: σ(z) = 1 / (1 + e⁻ᶻ) squashes scores into probabilities for classification.

questions.prompt: One-hot encoding is used to:

options.text: Convert categorical variables into binary columns

questions.explanation: One-hot creates a binary column per category, avoiding an implied ordering from integer codes.

questions.prompt: Why create interaction features like x₁·x₂?

options.text: Capture relationships linear models can't express with x₁ and x₂ alone

questions.explanation: Interaction terms let linear models represent multiplicative effects.

questions.prompt: K-fold cross-validation:

options.text: Trains k times, using each fold as validation once

questions.explanation: Each fold serves as validation once; results are averaged — a robust estimate of generalization.

questions.prompt: For heavily imbalanced classes, which metric best captures model performance?
questions.explanation: F1 balances precision and recall; PR-AUC focuses on the minority class.

questions.prompt: What is the primary purpose of randomization in experimental design?

options.text: Balance unknown confounders across treatment groups

questions.explanation: Random assignment makes groups statistically comparable on both observed and unobserved confounders.

questions.prompt: Statistical power (1 − β) is the probability of:

options.text: Detecting a true effect when it exists

questions.explanation: Power = 1 − β. Higher power means real effects are more likely to be detected.

questions.prompt: The main risk of peeking at A/B test results daily is:

options.text: Inflated false positive rate due to multiple comparisons

questions.explanation: Repeatedly checking p-values without correction inflates Type I error. Fix: fix the sample size up front or use sequential testing.

questions.prompt: Which best describes a Type I error?

options.text: Claiming an effect that doesn't exist (false positive)

questions.explanation: Type I = false positive (reject true H0); Type II = false negative (fail to reject false H0).

questions.prompt: K-means requires which input up front?
questions.explanation: K-means needs K fixed. Elbow method or silhouette score helps choose it.

questions.prompt: Which clustering algorithm does not require specifying K in advance?
questions.explanation: DBSCAN discovers clusters by density and can flag noise points.

questions.prompt: The main difference between ARIMA and exponential smoothing is:

options.text: ARIMA models autocorrelation explicitly; exponential smoothing weights recent observations more
Exponential smoothing only works for classification

questions.explanation: Both are classic time-series methods, but ARIMA models autoregressive and moving-average structure while exponential smoothing applies decaying weights.

questions.prompt: Seasonality in a time series means:

options.text: A repeating pattern at a fixed period (e.g., weekly, yearly)

questions.explanation: Seasonal patterns repeat at a fixed frequency. Trend is a long-term direction; seasonality is the cycle.

questions.prompt: Randomized controlled trials identify causal effects because:

options.text: Random assignment breaks the link between treatment and confounders

questions.explanation: Randomization makes treatment independent of both observed and unobserved confounders, giving unbiased effect estimates.

questions.prompt: Difference-in-differences estimates causal effects by comparing:

options.text: Change over time in a treated group vs change over time in a control group
A single group before and after

questions.explanation: DiD subtracts the control group's change from the treated group's change, differencing out common shocks.

questions.prompt: What is training-serving skew in production ML?

options.text: Differences in feature computation between training and production

questions.explanation: Even tiny differences (tokenizers, imputation, time zones) can make production behavior diverge from validation.

questions.prompt: Model drift means:

options.text: Model performance degrades over time as the world changes

questions.explanation: Data drift (P(X)) or concept drift (P(y|X)) reduces accuracy. Monitor and retrain as needed.

questions.prompt: When presenting to executives, which opening works best?

options.text: The recommended action or headline insight first

questions.explanation: Lead with the punchline. Executives want the decision; supporting detail follows for whoever asks.

questions.prompt: Which is the best way to communicate model uncertainty to stakeholders?

options.text: Quantify with confidence intervals or prediction intervals and explain the tradeoffs
Report a single point estimate only

questions.explanation: Communicating uncertainty helps stakeholders make better decisions and set realistic expectations.
